Freeze

Zara's mind had gone completely blank. Her recorder teacher, Mrs Alvi, watched anxiously from the front row. She raised her eyebrows, silently urging Zara to begin, but Zara's fingers wouldn't move. The hall lights felt impossibly bright. Somewhere in the third row, a chair creaked.

Zara closed her eyes, wishing the stage would simply swallow her whole.

The Windward Suite had been Zara's favourite piece since the very first time she'd heard it on the radio, in the car, on the way home from swimming lessons. She'd begged her parents for recorder lessons for almost a year before they finally agreed, and when Mrs Alvi asked who wanted to perform the hardest movement at the recital, Zara's hand had shot straight up before she could stop herself. Nobody else had even wanted to try.

Yet here she was, standing at the front of the hall, and not even ten seconds into the piece, everything had already fallen apart.

She could feel every single person in the audience watching her. Out of the corner of her eye, she noticed Mrs Alvi glancing towards Callum, who also knew the piece, ready to wave him up if Zara didn't start soon.

Come on, Zara, come on. What did the sheet music look like? With her eyes still shut, she pictured the opening bars: the curling black notes, the little swell mark above the third line, the page slightly creased at the corner from being folded into her school bag too many times. She pictured her own finger tracing along beneath the notes at home, again and again, until she knew the shape of the melody by heart.

And then, somehow, the notes came.

Zara lifted the recorder to her lips and played the opening phrase, low and steady. She could feel the audience settle, and the performance had truly begun.

Can self-driving cars fix our traffic problem?

If you have ever lived in a big city, you have probably spent plenty of time sitting at traffic lights. Traffic lights are a clever invention that let traffic move safely in every direction, but they come with a downside: when traffic builds up, cars spend long stretches waiting and only creep forward in short bursts.

Self-driving cars might offer a way to ease this problem. If cars could 'talk' directly to traffic lights, could intersections eventually need fewer lights, or none at all?

To test the idea, a team of engineers built a computer simulation of a busy intersection filled entirely with self-driving cars that could communicate directly with it.

The first system the researchers tried was fairly straightforward. As each car neared the intersection, it sent a signal ahead. The intersection would then reserve the next free gap for that car, and tell it exactly how much to slow down so it arrived at precisely the right moment to slot through safely. This system let cars move through faster than usual, and could handle much heavier traffic without long queues forming.

To push the number of cars through even further, the engineers tried something bolder: deliberately speeding some cars up and slowing others down so they clustered into small bunches all travelling the same way. This second system behaved a little like a miniature traffic light, letting one bunch through at a time. Crucially, though, the cars in each bunch never had to stop completely - they kept rolling the whole time. This second system moved roughly twice as many cars through the intersection as an ordinary traffic light setup.

Even so, don't expect real traffic lights to disappear any time soon. Both systems only work if every single car on the road is being driven by a computer rather than a person. But if driverless cars ever become the norm, it's possible that the traffic jam could eventually become a thing of the past.

The search

Marcus was on a mission. He had waited for this day for weeks, patiently planning and plotting. Now that the day had finally come, it was time to act.

'I know exactly what I need,' he murmured to himself, striding down the footpath through the busy Saturday crowds. 'And I know precisely where to find it.'

He marched straight past the chemist and the hardware store, past the shoe shop and the newsagent and the greengrocer. His mission would not be completed in any of those ordinary places. He didn't slow down or glance in a single window, but kept walking with purpose. His heart beat a little faster with excitement. He was about to find something that would make his sister's whole face light up, now that she was finally home from hospital and feeling better. And on such an important day, too. He could hardly stand the wait.

At last, he arrived outside a narrow shop with dusty windows and a faded sign above the door. A collection of wind-up toys sat in the window display, gathering a fine layer of dust, and a bell above the doorframe swung gently though nobody had touched it. A strange, papery smell drifted out from inside, like old cardboard and machine oil mixed together. Marcus breathed it in. Above the doorway, painted in peeling gold letters, was a single word: 'CURIOSITIES'.

Marcus pressed his face to the glass, scanning the crowded shelves inside, where oddities were arranged like specimens in a museum: brass telescopes, tangled kites, small clockwork animals frozen mid-stride. A treasure chest of forgotten things. But where was it? A flash of panic gripped him. It had definitely been here last week - surely nobody had already bought it? There! Right at the very back, perched high on a shelf, loftier than all the other treasures. A small wooden music box, carved with birds, with a single brass key on its side. Marcus grinned. It was perfect.

The old man who ran the shop had wiry grey eyebrows and wore round glasses pushed low on his nose. He looked as though he had wandered in from another century entirely. He was polishing a telescope lens when he noticed Marcus lingering outside the window. He peered over his glasses at him sharply.

Marcus checked his pocket to make sure his money was still there. He pushed open the door, and a little bell above it jingled. The old man set down the telescope. Unexpectedly, he broke into a warm smile, and his whole face creased into friendly wrinkles. 'Well now, young man. What can I help you find today?'

Swimming at the beach is about to feel a little creepier. Hidden in the shallow water of your local beach, and crawling through the coldest, deepest oceans on Earth, are sea spiders - strange, spindly creatures that look like they escaped from a science-fiction film. They range enormously in size, from less than a centimetre across to larger than a dinner plate, and with their tiny bodies and impossibly long legs, they're easy to imagine crawling all over you. But it gets stranger still.

Sea spiders feed using a long tube-like mouthpart called a proboscis, which they poke directly into the soft body of their prey before sucking out its insides. Surprisingly, many of these unlucky victims survive this gruesome attack. This is partly because the animals sea spiders usually prey on, such as sea sponges and sea anemones, tend to be considerably larger than the sea spider itself - so they can usually recover, at least most of the time.

In fact, their bodies are so small that many of their internal organs actually extend out into their legs instead. Many sea spiders living deep in the ocean have no need for eyes at all, and are completely blind.

Sea spiders puzzle scientists trying to classify them. They are not true spiders, since true spiders and other arachnids belong to a different animal group entirely. Instead, sea spiders have a hard, segmented outer shell, which places them among the arthropods - the same broad group as insects, crabs and true spiders. Their strange proboscis, though, makes it hard for scientists to agree on exactly where they fit within that group.

Marine biologist Dr Elena Brooks has spent years studying sea spiders, particularly the ones living in the icy waters of Antarctica. 'The Antarctic species tend to be bigger, stranger and far more varied than sea spiders found anywhere else on the planet - that's what makes them so fascinating to study,' she explains.

So next time you're exploring rock pools at the beach, look closely - you might just spot a tiny sea spider camouflaged among the seaweed. Don't worry, though: the truly enormous ones only live far away, in the depths of the Antarctic Ocean.

Alexey Leonov

On 18 March 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexey Leonov became the first person in history to walk in space. Connected to his spacecraft by a cable just over five metres long, he floated freely above Earth for around ten minutes. The achievement was a huge milestone for space exploration everywhere, and for the Soviet Union in particular, it was a source of enormous national pride that one of their own cosmonauts - rather than an American astronaut - had achieved it first.

Earlier that day, Leonov and fellow cosmonaut Pavel Belyayev had completed one full orbit of Earth aboard their two-person Voskhod spacecraft. Once the orbit was complete, mission control gave Leonov clearance to begin his spacewalk. He climbed into the airlock, opened the outer hatch, and pushed himself out into open space.

He later described the moment vividly: 'It was so quiet I could hear my own heartbeat. I was surrounded by stars, drifting with almost no control at all. I will never forget that feeling.' At the time, of course, he had no idea that the hardest part of the mission was still ahead of him: getting safely back inside.

In the vacuum of space, Leonov's spacesuit had ballooned outward dramatically, stretching and stiffening until it barely resembled its original shape. His hands slid loose inside his gloves, and his feet slipped free of his boots. Unable to fit back through the narrow airlock hatch in his swollen suit, Leonov made a split-second decision: he released some of the air from inside his suit, despite the serious risk of decompression sickness this created. 'I felt pins and needles running through my hands and legs,' he later recalled.

Even after Leonov successfully squeezed back inside the capsule, the mission's problems weren't over. Oxygen levels inside the cabin spiked to dangerously high levels, and during re-entry, the spacecraft's automatic guidance system failed completely. Relying on manual controls, skill and more than a little luck, the two cosmonauts landed almost 2000 kilometres off course, deep in a remote Siberian forest. Leonov and Belyayev then spent two freezing nights sheltering inside their capsule, listening for wolves, before rescuers finally reached them.

Back home, the mission was celebrated as an outstanding success. Still, the spacewalk had pushed Leonov to his physical limits, and the chaotic re-entry placed enormous strain on both cosmonauts and their equipment. Decades later, the dramatic events of the mission inspired a 2017 Russian film about the pioneering days of the space race.

The achievement was a huge milestone for space exploration everywhere, and for the Soviet Union in particular, it was a source of enormous national pride that one of their own cosmonauts - rather than an American astronaut - had achieved it first.

Earlier that day, Leonov and fellow cosmonaut Pavel Belyayev had completed one full orbit of Earth aboard their two-person Voskhod spacecraft. Once the orbit was complete, mission control gave Leonov clearance to begin his spacewalk. He climbed into the airlock, opened the outer hatch, and pushed himself out into open space.

He later described the moment vividly: 'It was so quiet I could hear my own heartbeat. I was surrounded by stars, drifting with almost no control at all. I will never forget that feeling.' At the time, of course, he had no idea that the hardest part of the mission was still ahead of him: getting safely back inside.

In the vacuum of space, Leonov's spacesuit had ballooned outward dramatically, stretching and stiffening until it barely resembled its original shape. His hands slid loose inside his gloves, and his feet slipped free of his boots. Unable to fit back through the narrow airlock hatch in his swollen suit, Leonov made a split-second decision: he released some of the air from inside his suit, despite the serious risk of decompression sickness this created. 'I felt pins and needles running through my hands and legs,' he later recalled.

Even after Leonov successfully squeezed back inside the capsule, the mission's problems weren't over. Oxygen levels inside the cabin spiked to dangerously high levels, and during re-entry, the spacecraft's automatic guidance system failed completely. Relying on manual controls, skill and more than a little luck, the two cosmonauts landed almost 2000 kilometres off course, deep in a remote Siberian forest. Leonov and Belyayev then spent two freezing nights sheltering inside their capsule, listening for wolves, before rescuers finally reached them.

Back home, the mission was celebrated as an outstanding success. The tunnel

It was my cousin Jed who laid the bet that, unlike him,
I'd never dare to cross the old drain beneath the hill alone.
I'm determined now to prove him wrong.

Wading reluctantly through the tall, wet grass,
I break the heavy quiet; hum a tune under my breath.
Searching for the entrance, I spot a crooked grin,
a black gap yawning between two slabs of stone.
My pulse is hammering; I'll wait a moment more.

Restless, my kelpie, without any warning, bolts on in,
but I am far too big and have to duck and shuffle
if I mean to enter this narrow tunnel at all.

At once I glimpse two amber, gleaming eyes -
a flash of fright, then dread dissolves to relief.
It's only Restless, waiting patiently up ahead.

The dark presses close, the damp air thick and warm.
I falter, then fumble for the torch inside my bag
and throw a thin beam along the crooked path.

We trace the tunnel through a weak and wavering light,
then all at once arrive somewhere vast and cool -
I freeze in wonder; it's suddenly, impossibly bright.

Thousands of tiny glow-worms shimmer like scattered stars,
lighting shapes of crystal in every shade of blue,
tall spires of stone rising, sharp and new.
Water drips in echoes from the ceiling high above.
Restless barks, the sound rolling on and on,
and in one sudden instant, I understand the truth.

What a strange and wonderful thing to find!
This is not the tunnel my cousin described to me at all.
Jed was never brave; he's never once gone in.
